lessons.title: Inside a clause

steps.headline: A clause is a finite verb and its subject, and you start with the verb.

lead.text: A finite verb is the one that changes with time: chases, chased. Ask who or what does it and you have the subject. Together they make a clause. Poetry often reorders its words, so find the verb first.
Sonnet 18 reorders its words, so position will not help you. Go by tense: which word would change if the line moved into the past?

reveal.text: You tested for tense. “Declines” becomes “declined”, so it is the verb. Ask who or what declines: “every fair” is the subject.

steps.headline: Is the last part of “The storm shook the roof” and of “The storm was fierce” an object or a complement?

lead.text: Some verbs pass their action on to a thing. Others only link the subject to a description.

workedSteps.text: Find the verb and subject in each: “the storm shook” and “the storm was”.
“Shook” acts on something: “the roof” receives the action, so it is an object.
“Was” only links the subject to what follows: “fierce” says what the storm is like, so it is a complement.

steps.headline: Find the head noun of the object in “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”.

reveal.text: You stripped the phrase back to its core. Every object is a phrase built round one noun, and the other words describe it.

workedSteps.text: Find the verb and its subject: “do shake” and “rough winds”.
Ask what the winds shake: “the darling buds of May”. That whole phrase is the object.
Take away the describing words and keep the one noun they describe.

lead.text: A clause with its own subject and verb can still fail to stand alone. A subordinator such as “when”, “because” or “which” makes it lean on another clause. Sonnet 130, line 3: “If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun.”

reveal.text: The little word at the front decided it. Independent clauses make sense alone; dependent ones wait for the rest.

parts.text: in disgrace with fortune and men's eyes

lead.text: Each clause has its own finite verb, so counting finite verbs counts clauses. Infinitives such as “to serve” and participles such as “despising” carry no tense and do not count.

reveal.text: You counted one verb for each clause. In long poetic sentences, that is the fastest way to see how the thought is built.

recap.keyIdea: Find the finite verb first, then its subject. What follows is an object or a complement, and a clause opening with “if” or “when” cannot stand alone.

blocks.text: You found “declines” as the verb in a Shakespeare line. Then you picked “buds” as the head of an object and counted the finite verbs in Sonnet 116.

lessons.title: Joining two clauses

steps.headline: The mark between two clauses says how they relate.

lead.text: A full stop keeps clauses apart. A semicolon links them as one thought. A comma links them only with a coordinating conjunction: “and” adds, “but” contrasts, “so” gives a result.
Read this as an editor would: “The vote was close, the motion failed.” It has two full clauses joined by a comma alone.

reveal.text: You were asked to name the fault. Editors call it a comma splice. Douglass's “You may rejoice, I must mourn” splices on purpose: the abrupt join makes two fates collide.

steps.headline: Repair “The rain stopped, the match began” in two ways.

workedSteps.text: Check each side. “The rain stopped” and “the match began” are both full clauses, so a comma alone cannot join them.
Option one: swap the comma for a semicolon. “The rain stopped; the match began.”
Option two: keep the comma and add a conjunction that fits. “The rain stopped, so the match began.”

steps.headline: Find the verb Douglass leaves out of his second and third clauses.

lead.text: Douglass joins three charges with semicolons. The second and third are shorter than the first.

reveal.text: The comma marks where the verb was dropped. Commas inside each clause are already busy, so the semicolons separate the clauses.

workedSteps.text: Read the first clause whole: “To him, your celebration is a sham;”
The second clause has a subject, “your boasted liberty”, and a complement, “an unholy license”, but no verb.
Which verb from the first clause is understood here?

lead.text: A colon follows a complete clause and promises that what comes next will explain or specify it. Sonnet 18 ends line 2 with one, and the lines after it set out why summer falls short. The words before a colon must be able to stand as a sentence.

reveal.text: You tested the words before each colon. Only a complete clause can make the promise that the second part keeps.

lead.text: A dash breaks harder than a comma. Lincoln's Bliss copy uses dashes to separate “we can not dedicate” from “we can not consecrate”, forcing a pause before each stronger verb. Now repair a plain splice.

reveal.text: The second clause is the result of the first, so the conjunction names the relation that the comma left out.

recap.keyIdea: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses. Choose a semicolon, a colon, a dash or a conjunction by the relation you mean.

lessons.title: Actors and actions

steps.headline: Put the actor in the subject and the action in the verb.

lead.text: In the active voice the subject acts: “The committee rejected the motion.” The passive makes the receiver the subject: “The motion was rejected by the committee.” It builds the verb from “be” plus a past participle, and the actor moves to a “by” phrase or vanishes.
“The motion was rejected by the committee” makes the receiver its subject. Rewrite it so the committee acts, then count the words of your version.

reveal.text: You moved the actor to the front and dropped “was” and “by”. The passive's extra words disappeared, and the sentence now opens with whoever acted.

steps.headline: Make “The report was written by the analyst” active.

workedSteps.text: Find the actor. The “by” phrase names the analyst.
Make the actor the subject: “The analyst”.
Turn “was written” into a plain past verb and keep the receiver as its object: “The analyst wrote the report.”

steps.headline: Make “Mistakes were made by the finance office” active.

lead.text: The passive can delete the actor altogether. That is honest when nobody knows who acted, and evasive when the writer does.

reveal.text: The actor was in the sentence all along, hidden behind “by”. Ask of every passive: who did this, and should the reader know?

workedSteps.text: The receiver is “mistakes”, and the verb is “were made”.
The actor is named inside the “by” phrase.
Move the actor to the front. Which words become the subject?

steps.headline: A nominalisation buries a verb inside a noun.

lead.text: “Refuse” becomes “a refusal”, and “decide” becomes “a decision”. The noun then needs a weak verb such as “gave” or “made” to carry it. The sentence gains words and loses force. Turn the noun back into a verb and both come back.
Look for a noun that is really an action, and for the weak verb propping it up. Make the committee the actor.

reveal.text: You turned two noun phrases back into verbs. Fewer words, and the committee now does something.

lead.text: Some words carry no meaning a reader would miss. A phrase like “in my opinion, it is true that” only announces a claim, and a modifier can repeat what the noun already says. Count the sentence before you cut.

reveal.text: The claim stayed and ten words went. A revision that loses words and keeps the claim is an improvement you can measure.

lessons.orientation: Move actors into subjects and actions into verbs. Switch between active and passive, unbury nominalisations and count the words a revision saves.

recap.keyIdea: Make the actor the subject and the action the verb. Unbury verbs from nouns and cut words that carry no meaning.

lessons.title: Claim, grounds and warrant

steps.headline: A claim needs grounds, and a warrant to link the grounds to it.

lead.text: Toulmin's model of argument (1958) starts with three parts. The claim is the conclusion. The grounds are the facts offered for it. The warrant is the general rule that licenses the step. “Pick Mia, because she scored 20 goals” rests on the unstated rule that high scorers help a team.
Three statements follow. Ask which one the other two are offered to support.

reveal.text: You looked for the conclusion. The claim is the statement the others are reasons for: here, closing the bridge.

statements.text: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.
The museum should open late every Thursday.
Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.
A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost.
The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last.

steps.headline: Label the parts of: “Rain is forecast, so take a coat, since forecasts are usually right.”

workedSteps.text: Find the conclusion. “Take a coat” is what the writer wants accepted, so it is the claim.
Find the fact offered for it. “Rain is forecast” is a particular fact, so it is the grounds.
Ask what rule links the two. “Forecasts are usually right” is general, so it is the warrant.

steps.headline: Label the rule behind: “His fingerprints were on the knife, so he handled it.”

lead.text: Attacking the rule behind an argument is often stronger than attacking its facts. Nobody disputes the prints. A lawyer asks what they prove.

reveal.text: Writing the rule out shows what the argument assumes. Once it is written, a lawyer can ask whether prints show handling at the relevant time.

workedSteps.text: The claim is “he handled the knife”.
The grounds are “his fingerprints were on the knife”.
Name the unstated rule that links the two.

statements.text: The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
Forensic studies show that ridge patterns are individual and transfer by contact.

steps.headline: Qualifiers and rebuttals limit a claim, and backing supports the warrant.

lead.text: A qualifier states how strongly the claim is made: “in most cases”, “almost certainly”. A rebuttal names the conditions under which it would fail, often after “unless”. Backing is different: it supports the warrant itself, as a safety code does for an engineering rule.
Read the sentence for the word that measures how sure the writer is, and for the clause that names what could go wrong.

reveal.text: You separated the two. A qualifier and a rebuttal concede in advance the exceptions an opponent would raise, so the claim is harder to knock down.

statements.text: Harriet leads every poll by eight points.
Probably.
Harriet will win the election.
Unless rain keeps her supporters at home.
The air pressure is falling fast.
Very likely.
It will rain tomorrow.
Unless the front stalls over the coast.

lead.text: Label each statement by the job it does. A particular observation is grounds. A general rule linking it to the conclusion is the warrant. An “unless” clause is a rebuttal.

reveal.text: Sorting by job shows the shape: a fact, a general rule, a conclusion and an exception. Only one statement is a general rule.

statements.text: Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise.
Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.
The price should return to its old level.
Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen.
The museum should open late every Thursday.
Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.
A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost.
The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last.

lessons.title: Ethos, pathos, logos and kairos

steps.headline: A speech persuades through the speaker, the audience's feelings and the argument.

lead.text: Aristotle's Rhetoric names three proofs. Ethos is the speaker's character and credibility. Pathos is the feeling a speech arouses in its hearers. Logos is the argument carried by the words.
Douglass speaks in Rochester in 1852 as a man who escaped slavery, to an audience celebrating Independence Day. He says: “This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.” What gives him the right?

reveal.text: His standing as someone who lived what he describes is his proof. That is ethos. Lincoln builds it differently, with “we”: the president speaks as one of the mourners, not above them.

spans.text: I am not included within the pale of this glorious anniversary!
This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.
You may rejoice, I must mourn.
We have come to dedicate a portion of that field,
as a final resting place for those who here gave their lives that that nation might live.

steps.headline: Name the appeals in: “As a lifelong farmer, I ask you to picture the empty field next spring.”

workedSteps.text: Split the sentence by what each part works on.
“As a lifelong farmer” says who is speaking and why to trust her. That is ethos.
“Picture the empty field” asks you to feel a loss. That is pathos.

steps.headline: Name the appeal in Douglass's contrast between two outcomes of one sunlight.

lead.text: Douglass sets one sunlight against two outcomes. “Stripes” are the marks of the whip, placed beside the audience's own “life and healing”.

reveal.text: The contrast is physical, so the feeling is hard to avoid. Lincoln's version is quieter: the dead gave “the last full measure of devotion”, and the living are asked to be worthy of it.

workedSteps.text: The audience hears two images side by side: one warm, one cruel.
The image is chosen to move the listeners, not to prove a point.
Name the appeal that works through the audience's feelings.

spans.text: The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.
that from these honored dead we take increased devotion to that cause for which they gave
the last full measure of devotion

lead.text: Lincoln opens with a founding premise and dates the nation from a founding document, not the Constitution. He speaks in November 1863. Work out the year that “Four score and seven years ago” points to.

reveal.text: The year belongs to the Declaration of Independence, so Lincoln rests the nation on its founding premise rather than on the Constitution. From that premise he argues what the war tests, which is logos.

spans.text: Four score and seven years ago
our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and
dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
Now we are engaged in a great civil war,
testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.

steps.headline: Kairos is the fit between an argument and its moment.

lead.text: Kairos is the opportune moment: what makes an argument fit its occasion and place. A speaker may turn the occasion into the subject, or use the place itself as evidence.
Douglass, invited to speak at an Independence Day celebration in Rochester, turns the occasion into his subject: “What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?”

reveal.text: He made the holiday's own meaning the argument. Lincoln did the same with the ground: “We are met on a great battle-field of that war” uses the place itself as evidence.

spans.text: What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?
I answer, a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.
We are met on a great battle-field of that war.

lessons.title: Figures of repetition and balance

steps.headline: Repeating an opening and matching opposites both give a sentence a frame to hold on to.

lead.text: Anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses, so attention moves to what changes inside the frame. Antithesis places opposed ideas in parallel grammatical form, so the parallel sharpens the opposition.
Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities with one sentence that keeps a single frame going for ten clauses. Here is its start. Count how often the frame opens a clause.

reveal.text: Four times in this extract. The repeated opening is anaphora: the frame stays still while best and worst, wisdom and foolishness change inside it. Douglass uses “your” the same way, and each repetition points back at his audience.

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

steps.headline: Name the figure in Lincoln's “what we say here” against “what they did here”.

lead.text: Lincoln sets two halves in one grammatical frame. Only the opposed words change.

reveal.text: The matching frame makes the opposition collide, so the speech enacts its own modesty: words matter less than deeds. Dickens's “best” and “worst” sit in the same slot of the same clause.

workedSteps.text: Put the two halves side by side: “what we say here” and “what they did here”.
The grammar is identical. Only the words change: “we” against “they”, saying against doing.
Name the figure that balances opposed ideas in parallel form.

spans.text: The world will little note, nor long remember

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

steps.headline: Chiasmus reverses its terms, and a tricolon runs three members in step.

lead.text: Chiasmus repeats terms in reverse order, A B then B A. Lines drawn between the matching words cross like the Greek letter chi. When the same words return it is strictly antimetabole. A tricolon is a series of three parallel members.
Douglass places this at the turning point of his Narrative, just before he fights back against Covey. The grammar reverses as his life does. Look at the order of the terms in each half.

reveal.text: The terms return reversed: man, slave, then slave, man. Because the same words come back, the stricter name is antimetabole.

lead.text: Lincoln's close varies only the preposition: “of the people, by the people, for the people”. Each phrase adds a relation: government drawn from the people, run by them, serving them.

reveal.text: Three parallel members make a tricolon. His earlier verbs, “dedicate”, “consecrate” and “hallow”, climb from civic to sacred, so those members grow in weight.

spans.text: shall not perish from the earth.
But, in a larger sense, we can not

lessons.title: Metre and scansion

steps.headline: Verse has a beat, and an iamb puts it on the second syllable of each pair.

lead.text: Scansion starts with syllables. An unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one is an iamb. Five iambs make iambic pentameter, the line of English verse drama and of the sonnet: ten syllables, with the beats on every second one.
Say Sonnet 18's first line slowly, and tap once for each vowel sound. Do not count words; count syllables.

reveal.text: Ten, with the beats on I, pare, to, sum and day. “To” takes a beat only because of where it stands: metrical stress need not match speech.

steps.headline: Scan “They also serve who only stand and waite”.

workedSteps.text: Count the syllables: they, al, so, serve, who, on, ly, stand, and, waite. Ten.
Mark weak and strong in turn, starting weak: they AL so SERVE who ON ly STAND and WAITE.
The five beats sit on every second syllable, so the line is iambic pentameter.

steps.headline: Place the beats of “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”.

lead.text: Spoken English rarely gives five equal stresses. “Rough” is heavy too, and reading it against the metre is part of the line's force.

reveal.text: You stepped through the line two syllables at a time. The rhythm is regular, and the light words sit between the heavy ones.

workedSteps.text: Count ten syllables: rough, winds, do, shake, the, dar, ling, buds, of, May.
The first beat is on “winds” and the second on “shake”.
Keep going in steps of two syllables.

lead.text: A line can carry an extra unstressed syllable after its last beat. Sonnet 116 has one in line 6. Count carefully, tapping once for each vowel sound.

reveal.text: “-ken” trails after the last beat on “sha-”. This is a feminine ending, and the line is still pentameter because it keeps five beats. Hamlet's “To be, or not to be, that is the question” has the same shape.

steps.headline: Reverse the iamb to get a trochee, and count the feet to name the metre.

lead.text: A trochee is a stressed syllable then an unstressed one, the reverse of an iamb. A line is named by its number of feet: three is trimeter, four tetrameter and five pentameter.

Dickinson's iambic “And sings the tune without the words” has eight syllables and four beats, and it rises. The witches chant to a different beat, one that falls. Their line has the same number of strong syllables.

reveal.text: The witches chant in trochaic tetrameter: DOU-ble DOU-ble TOIL and TROU-ble. Each foot falls, and the last unstressed syllable is dropped. Shakespeare gives his supernatural speakers a metre unlike his humans' iambic speech.

lessons.orientation: Count syllables and place the beats of iambic pentameter. Hear a feminine ending, and tell a rising iamb from a falling trochee.

recap.keyIdea: Metre is a pattern of weak and strong syllables. Iambic pentameter has five iambs, ten syllables and beats on the even ones.

lessons.title: Sound and image

steps.headline: Alliteration repeats a consonant sound, and assonance repeats a vowel sound.

lead.text: Alliteration repeats a consonant sound at the start of nearby words, usually on stressed syllables. Assonance repeats a vowel sound inside nearby stressed syllables, whatever the consonants. Both belong to sound, not spelling: “cider” and “sorrow” alliterate, “cider” and “cat” do not.
Sonnet 30 opens: “When to the sessions of sweet silent thought”. Say it aloud and listen to how each word begins.

reveal.text: Three words share the opening sound: sessions, sweet and silent. The hushed s suits a line about silent thought. Keats opens “To Autumn” with “mists and mellow”, two m sounds that slow the line.

steps.headline: Count the long i sounds in Keats's “Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness”.

lead.text: Assonance follows the sound of a vowel, whatever the spelling. Say each word aloud.

reveal.text: The long vowel of “bride” returns in “qui-”, binding the urn's two names together. Shakespeare's “new wail my dear time's waste” sounds the vowel of “wail” again in “waste”.

workedSteps.text: The model word is “bride”, with the long vowel of “time”.
“Still” and “unravish'd” have the short vowel of “sit”, so they do not match.
Count the words with the long vowel of “bride”, the model word included.

model.source: Keats, 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', line 1

steps.headline: A simile compares openly, and a metaphor identifies one thing with another.

lead.text: A simile compares with “like” or “as”: the word keeps the two things apart. A metaphor asserts that one thing is another, with no such word. Then it can build on the assertion, as in “The classroom was a zoo”.
Burns writes “O my Luve's like a red, red rose.” Look for the word that tells you how the comparison is made.

reveal.text: “Like” keeps the two things apart: his love resembles a rose. Romeo does something stronger with “Juliet is the sun”. He asserts it, then tells the “fair sun” to “kill the envious moon”.

spans.text: But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?

lessons.title: The sonnet and its turn

steps.headline: A rhyme scheme gives each rhyme sound a letter, and a sonnet fixes the pattern.

lead.text: Lines with the same letter rhyme: ABAB rhymes lines 1 and 3, and lines 2 and 4. A Shakespearean sonnet has fourteen lines of iambic pentameter: three quatrains of four lines and a closing couplet of two. A Petrarchan sonnet splits into an octave of eight lines and a sestet of six.
Each quatrain of a Shakespearean sonnet brings rhymes of its own, and the couplet answers them. Sonnet 18 ends: “So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.”

reveal.text: Seven, A to G. Each quatrain brings two new rhymes and the couplet adds one, so the poem moves through seven sounds and ends on a pair.

lines.text: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature’s changing course untrimm’d:
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st,
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
When I consider how my light is spent,
E’re half my days, in this dark world and wide,
And that one Talent which is death to hide,
Lodg’d with me useless, though my Soul more bent
To serve therewith my Maker, and present
My true account, least he returning chide,
Doth God exact day-labour, light deny’d,
I fondly ask; But patience to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, God doth not need
Either man’s work or his own gifts, who best
Bear his milde yoak, they serve him best, his State
Is Kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed
And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest:
They also serve who only stand and waite.

steps.headline: Count the rhyme sounds in the octave of Milton's “When I consider how my light is spent”.

lead.text: Four rhymes on one sound are easy in Italian and hard in English, so a Petrarchan octave is a demanding form.

reveal.text: Two sounds carry all eight lines. Milton keeps the Italian pattern even though English supplies such rhymes with difficulty.

workedSteps.text: The octave's eight line endings: spent, wide, hide, bent, present, chide, deny'd, prevent.
Lines 1, 4, 5 and 8 share one ending sound, and lines 2, 3, 6 and 7 share another.
The octave rhymes ABBAABBA. Count the distinct letters.

And that one Talent which is death to hide,
Lodg’d with me useless, though my Soul more bent

My true account, least he returning chide,

And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest:

My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun;
Coral is far more red, than her lips red:
If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun;
If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.
I have seen roses damask’d, red and white,
But no such roses see I in her cheeks;
And in some perfumes is there more delight
Than in the breath that from my mistress reeks.
I love to hear her speak, yet well I know
That music hath a far more pleasing sound:
I grant I never saw a goddess go;
My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground:
And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare,
As any she belied with false compare.

steps.headline: The volta is the turn where a sonnet changes direction.

lead.text: The volta moves a sonnet from problem to answer, or from complaint to consolation. In a Petrarchan sonnet it usually falls where the octave gives way to the sestet.
Sonnet 29 spends its opening quatrains on envy and self-pity. Read for the first word that changes direction, and count down to its line.

reveal.text: Line 9: “Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising”. After eight lines of envy and self-pity, “Yet” turns the poem, and the speaker's state rises “like to the lark at break of day arising”.

lines.text: When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes
I all alone beweep my outcast state,
And trouble deaf heaven with my bootless cries,
And look upon myself, and curse my fate,
Wishing me like to one more rich in hope,
Featur’d like him, like him with friends possess’d,
Desiring this man’s art, and that man’s scope,
With what I most enjoy contented least;
Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising,
Haply I think on thee, and then my state,
Like to the lark at break of day arising
From sullen earth, sings hymns at heaven’s gate;
For thy sweet love remember’d such wealth brings
That then I scorn to change my state with kings.
Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature’s changing course untrimm’d:

Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

lead.text: Shakespeare often delays the turn to the couplet. Sonnet 130 refuses every flattering comparison for three quatrains.

reveal.text: The couplet carries the turn: “And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare”. Milton turns early, in line 8: “But patience to prevent / That murmur, soon replies”. Where the turn falls decides how much of the poem argues and how much answers.

steps.headline: Grammatical person tells you where the narrator stands.

lead.text: A first-person narrator is a character who says “I”, as Poe's does. A third-person narrator stands outside the story and calls the characters “he” and “she”. An omniscient third-person narrator can also generalise beyond any one mind.
Emma opens with a narrator who describes its heroine. Ask whether the narrator ever speaks as a character, and notice how much the word “seemed” suggests it knows.

reveal.text: Third person: the narrator names Emma and calls her “she”. “Seemed” already hints that this narrator knows more than Emma does. Poe's narrator, by contrast, says “why will you say that I am mad?”

spans.text: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence;
True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?

lead.text: An omniscient narrator can generalise beyond any one mind. Pride and Prejudice opens with a claim about what is “universally acknowledged”. Ask who is speaking, and whose assumption it is.

reveal.text: The narrator voices a neighbourhood's assumption with irony. The next paragraph shows the “surrounding families” regarding a rich newcomer as “the rightful property” of their daughters, so the wanting runs the other way.

spans.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged,
that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.
this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as

steps.headline: Free indirect discourse puts a character's thought into the narrator's grammar.

lead.text: The narrator keeps third person and past tense, but the character's exclamation, question or idiom enters the sentence with no “she thought that”. There are no quotation marks, so the reader moves between minds without a signal.

steps.headline: Turn Anna's thought “What a dreadful day this has been!” into free indirect discourse.

workedSteps.text: Start from the direct thought, in her words and her person: “What a dreadful day this has been!”
Move to the narrator's grammar: third person and past tense.
Keep her exclamation and drop the reporting words. “What a dreadful day it had been!”

lead.text: After Mr Elton's proposal, Austen writes: “Emma sat down to think and be miserable. It was a wretched business indeed!” The second sentence is Emma's exclamation, not the narrator's verdict.

reveal.text: The narrator's grammar carries Emma's voice, so readers share her mistakes before they recognise them as mistakes.

spans.text: The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
It was a wretched business indeed!
“If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
How she could have been so deceived!

lead.text: Two questions sort the modes: who is speaking, and whose words are these? Quotation marks mark direct speech. Actions reported from outside are plain narration.

reveal.text: “How she could have been so deceived!” is Emma's exclamation in the narrator's third person and past tense. No reporting verb or quotation marks frame it.

spans.text: (1) “If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
(2) The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
(3) How she could have been so deceived!
Such an overthrow of every thing she had been wishing for!
She looked back as well as she could;

lessons.title: Irony and unreliable narrators

steps.headline: Verbal irony says one thing and means another, and the audience hears the gap.

lead.text: Irony is a gap between what is said or expected and what is meant or what happens. In verbal irony a speaker says one thing and means another. The gap works only if the audience can hear it: a repeated word can turn against the person it praises.
Mark Antony speaks to the crowd after Caesar's murder. Brutus has called Caesar ambitious. In the lines shown Antony keeps returning to one phrase about Brutus. Count how often it comes.

reveal.text: Four times. Each repetition follows evidence against the charge of ambition: the captives' ransoms, the refused crown. By the last repetition the word has turned against Brutus, and the crowd has done the turning.

spans.text: So are they all, all honourable men,
But Brutus says he was ambitious,
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: For Brutus is an honourable man.
model.said: Brutus is honourable, and so his charge that Caesar was ambitious must be true.
model.known: Brutus helped kill Caesar, and each repetition invites the crowd to doubt the word.

steps.headline: Dramatic irony depends on what the audience knows, situational irony on what happens.

lead.text: In dramatic irony the audience knows something a character does not, so the character's words carry more meaning for us. In situational irony an outcome reverses the intention or expectation behind it. Neither needs a speaker to say the opposite.
Romeo marvels that death “hath had no power yet upon thy beauty”. Think about what the audience knows that Romeo does not.

reveal.text: Every line Romeo speaks means more to us than to him, because unequal knowledge drives the irony. Duncan's “This castle hath a pleasant seat” works the same way, spoken by a king the audience knows will be murdered inside it.

model.speaker: Romeo
model.line: Death that hath suck’d the honey of thy breath, / Hath had no power yet upon thy beauty.
model.said: Juliet is dead, and her beauty is death's strange mercy.
model.known: Juliet has taken the Friar's sleeping potion and is about to wake.

model.speaker: Duncan
model.line: This castle hath a pleasant seat.
model.said: The castle is a welcoming place to rest.
model.known: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth have resolved to murder Duncan there that night.

lead.text: Romeo steps between the duellists to make peace. Later, to the dying Mercutio, he says: “I thought all for the best.”

reveal.text: The outcome turns against its cause: peace-making gives Tybalt his opening. This kind of irony needs no speaker and no hidden knowledge, only an outcome that reverses its purpose.

model.speaker: Romeo
model.line: I thought all for the best.
model.said: Stepping between the fighters will stop the duel.
model.known: Tybalt's thrust under Romeo's arm kills Mercutio: the peace-making makes the death possible.

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: And sure he is an honourable man.
model.known: Antony means the opposite, and the crowd hears it.

lead.text: Poe's narrator protests his calm in sentences broken by dashes and repetition. He offers his acute hearing, “I heard many things in hell”, as proof of sanity. Wayne Booth named this type of narrator in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961).

reveal.text: The reader learns to doubt the account from evidence inside the telling, and assembles a second story from what the narrator lets slip.

but why will you say that I am mad?
I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell.
Object there was none. Passion there was none.

steps.headline: Freytag shaped a five-act play like a pyramid: it climbs to a peak and falls away.

lead.text: Gustav Freytag's Die Technik des Dramas (1863) divides a five-act play into five parts. They run from the introduction and the rise to the climax, then the return or fall and the catastrophe. The climax is the highest point, where the protagonist's fortunes stop rising and start to fall.
Look at Romeo and Juliet by act. Freytag read it as a pyramid. Ask in which act the fortunes stop rising and start to fall.

reveal.text: Act 3. Freytag traces the rise through four stages: the masked ball, the garden, the wedding and Tybalt's death. He sets the climax in Act 3, from Juliet's “Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds” to Romeo's farewell. Everything after it descends towards the tomb.

lead.text: Freytag's first part sets out the world before the action starts. For Romeo and Juliet that is an Italian city where swords are worn and quarrels flare, ruled by a prince who keeps the peace with difficulty.

reveal.text: The opening part, which English critics usually call the exposition, sets out the world before the action starts. It ends at the exciting moment: Romeo and his friends deciding to go to the Capulet feast.

questions.prompt: Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 says 'And every fair from fair sometime declines.' Which single word is the finite verb?
hints: Put the line into the past tense. Which word changes form?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Declines' is the finite verb: it carries tense and would become 'declined' in the past. Its subject is 'every fair'.

questions.onCorrect: “Declines” is the verb: it would become “declined” in the past. Its subject is “every fair”.

misconceptions.feedback: That word names the subject or places the action. Put the line into the past and see which word has to change.

questions.prompt: In 'Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May', the object is a noun phrase. What is its head noun, the one word the rest of the phrase describes?
hints: Strip away the describing words. Which noun is left as the thing being shaken?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The object is 'the darling buds of May'; its head noun is 'buds'. 'Darling' and 'of May' modify it.

questions.onCorrect: The head of “the darling buds of May” is “buds”. “Darling” and “of May” only describe it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Darling” describes the noun. Find the noun that the other words are describing.
“May” sits inside “of May”, which describes the thing shaken rather than naming it.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 130 has 'If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun.' Which word makes the first clause dependent?
hints: Which word turns a statement into a condition?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'If' subordinates 'snow be white', so that clause cannot stand alone; 'her breasts are dun' can.

questions.onCorrect: “If” turns “snow be white” into a condition, so that clause cannot stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the clause's own content. Look for the small word in front that makes it wait for an answer.

questions.prompt: How many finite verbs are in 'Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds'?
hints: A finite verb carries tense: test each word by putting the lines into the past.
Check the main clause, then the clause opened by 'which', then the clause opened by 'when'.
List one verb from each clause and count the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'is', 'alters' and 'finds'. Each anchors a clause.

questions.onCorrect: Three: “is”, “alters” and “finds”. Each finite verb anchors its own clause.

misconceptions.feedback: Two clauses are easy to see, but the clause opened by “when” has a verb of its own.
That counts only the main clause. The clauses opened by “which” and “when” each have a verb.
Check that every word you counted carries tense. A noun is not a verb.

questions.prompt: Douglass, 1852: 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.' How many independent clauses does this sentence hold?
hints: Find each subject and finite verb pair.
Ask whether each clause could stand as a sentence on its own.
Neither clause opens with a subordinator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'You may rejoice' and 'I must mourn'. Each could stand alone, and the comma between them is a deliberate splice.

questions.onCorrect: Two: “You may rejoice” and “I must mourn”. Each has its own subject and verb and could stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a second subject with its own verb. A comma does not fuse two clauses into one.
Pair each subject with its finite verb. “May” and “must” belong to the verbs beside them.

questions.prompt: In Lincoln's 'The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here', what is the grammatical function of 'what we say here'?
hints: Ask: the world will little note what? The answer names the object.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'What we say here' is a noun clause that receives the action of 'note' and 'remember', so it is their object. The subject is 'the world'.

questions.onCorrect: “What we say here” is what the world will note and remember, so it is the object of both verbs.

misconceptions.feedback: The subject does the noting. Ask what is noted: that is the clause in question.
A complement follows a linking verb and describes the subject. “Note” and “remember” act on something.

questions.prompt: 'The vote was close, the motion failed.' Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone. What do editors call this construction?
hints: The name pairs the mark with a word from rope-work and film editing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A comma splice: in edited prose a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

questions.onCorrect: A comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses in edited prose.

misconceptions.feedback: A run-on has no punctuation at all between the clauses. Here a comma is present.
A fragment lacks a subject or a verb. Both halves here are complete clauses.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.' Which verb is understood but not repeated in the second and third clauses?
hints: Read the first clause, then lend its verb to the second.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Is': each later clause means 'your boasted liberty is an unholy license'. The comma marks where the verb was left out.

questions.onCorrect: “Is” is understood in the later clauses. The comma marks the gap where it was left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a subject or a complement, not a verb. Find the verb the first clause lends to the others.
The missing verb is borrowed from the first clause exactly as it stands there.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
hints: Test the words before each colon: could they stand as a sentence?

acceptedIdeas: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A colon needs a complete clause before it, and what follows should explain or specify. Only the first sentence meets both conditions.

choices.label: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
The motion: failed by two votes.
The reasons were: cost and delay.

questions.onCorrect: A colon needs a full clause before it, and what follows should explain it. Only this sentence meets both.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the words before the colon: “The motion” cannot stand as a sentence.
“The reasons were” cannot stand as a sentence, so a colon after it is misplaced.

questions.prompt: Repair 'It was late, we left' by keeping the comma and adding a coordinating conjunction that states cause and result. Which conjunction do you add?
hints: The second clause is the result of the first. Which short word introduces a result?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'So': 'It was late, so we left.' 'And' would join the clauses without naming the cause.

questions.onCorrect: “So” names the result. “It was late, so we left” says why they left, which “and” would not.

misconceptions.feedback: “And” only adds a second fact. Ask how the second clause relates to the first.
“But” signals contrast. Here the second clause follows from the first.
“Because” opens a dependent clause and would not follow a comma here. Use a coordinating conjunction.

questions.prompt: Douglass writes 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.' Keeping the comma, which coordinating conjunction would make this standard edited prose while keeping the contrast?
hints: Choose the conjunction that sets one clause against the other.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'But' or 'yet': 'You may rejoice, but I must mourn.' Both name the contrast; 'and' would flatten it.

questions.onCorrect: “But” sets one clause against the other. “Yet” does the same job.

misconceptions.feedback: “And” would flatten the contrast into a plain addition.
“So” gives a result, and rejoicing does not cause mourning.

Check whether any clause opens with a subordinator such as 'because' or 'when'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'The hall was full', 'the speaker was late' and 'his train had stopped outside the city'. The colon introduces the reason for the lateness.

questions.onCorrect: Three: each of the three clauses has its own subject and verb, and the marks separate them.

misconceptions.feedback: Two is close. Check the part after the colon: it is a full clause too.
Each mark here separates complete clauses, so there is more than one.
Count only subject-and-verb pairs, and check that each could stand as a sentence.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'The motion was rejected by the committee' in the active voice. How many words does the active sentence have?

questions.onCorrect: Five words: “The committee rejected the motion.” The actor leads and the passive's extra words go.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the passive's own length. Rewrite it with the committee acting, then count.

That is the length of the revision. Subtract it from the original.

questions.prompt: Cut the empty frame 'In my opinion, it is true that' and the redundant words 'personal', 'basically' and 'final' from 'In my personal opinion, it is basically true that the final outcome depends on the weather.' How many words remain?

That is the original length. Remove the frame and the repeated words first.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the passive's own length. Count the active version and subtract.

questions.prompt: Three statements: 'Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.' 'The bridge should close to lorries.' 'A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.' Which is the claim?

choices.label: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.

questions.onCorrect: The bridge should close to lorries: the other two statements are offered as its reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a fact offered in support. Ask which statement the others are reasons for.

questions.prompt: Grounds: 'The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.' Claim: 'The defendant handled the knife.' What is Toulmin's name for the unstated rule 'Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it'?

questions.onCorrect: The warrant is the general principle that authorises the move from these grounds to this claim.

misconceptions.feedback: The claim is the conclusion, here the statement about handling. Name the rule that links the fact to it.
The grounds are the fingerprints themselves. The question asks for the rule behind the step.

questions.prompt: In 'Harriet will probably win, unless rain keeps her supporters at home', which single word is the qualifier?
hints: Find the word that measures how confident the claim is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Probably' limits the force of the claim; 'unless rain keeps her supporters at home' is the rebuttal, the condition under which it fails.

misconceptions.feedback: That part names what could go wrong. Find the word that measures how sure the writer is.

questions.prompt: Statements: (1) Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise. (2) Customers buy less of a product when its price rises. (3) The price should return to its old level. (4) Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen. Give the number of the statement that is the warrant.
hints: Find the claim first: the statement the others support.
Find the observed fact; that is the grounds.
The warrant is a general rule rather than a particular fact.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Statement 2 is the warrant: a general rule linking the sales figure (grounds, statement 1) to the pricing claim (statement 3). Statement 4 is the rebuttal.

questions.onCorrect: Statement 2 is the warrant: a general rule linking the sales figure to the pricing claim.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a particular observed fact, so it supplies the grounds.
That is what the writer wants accepted: the claim.
That names exceptions that would limit the argument, so it is a rebuttal.

questions.prompt: Statements: (1) The museum should open late every Thursday. (2) Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late. (3) A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost. (4) The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last. Give the number of the statement that supplies the grounds.
hints: Find the statement the others support.
Grounds are particular observed facts, not general rules.
The last statement limits the argument rather than supporting it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Statement 2 supplies the grounds: an observed fact. Statement 1 is the claim, 3 the warrant and 4 a rebuttal.

questions.onCorrect: Statement 2 is an observed fact, so it supplies the grounds for the claim in statement 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the others support, so it is the claim.
That is a general rule, not an observed fact.
That limits the argument. It does not support it.

questions.prompt: A writer supports the warrant 'Damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads' by citing the national bridge inspection code. In Toulmin's model, what is that support called?
hints: The support is aimed at the rule, not at the conclusion.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Backing: support for the warrant itself, as opposed to grounds, which support the claim.

questions.onCorrect: Backing supports the warrant itself, as opposed to grounds, which support the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: Grounds support the claim. This support is aimed at the rule behind it.

questions.prompt: Douglass tells his Rochester audience, 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.' His right to say it rests on his own life as a man who had escaped slavery. Which of Aristotle's appeals works through the speaker's character and standing?
hints: The Greek word is the root of 'ethics'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: the persuasive force of the speaker's character and credibility.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos: Douglass's own life as a man who had escaped slavery gives him the standing to say it.

misconceptions.feedback: Pathos works on the audience's feelings. Here the force comes from who is speaking.

questions.prompt: 'The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.' The image of 'stripes and death' is aimed chiefly at the audience's feelings. Which appeal is this?
hints: The Greek root also gives English 'sympathy'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos: the appeal to the audience's emotions, here pity and shame.

questions.onCorrect: Pathos: “stripes and death” is chosen to move the hearers, and it makes the contrast physical.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos is about the speaker's standing. This image is aimed at the hearers' feelings.
Nothing here is reasoned from premise to consequence. The image is chosen to move the audience.

questions.prompt: Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg in November 1863. 'Four score and seven years ago' points back to which year?
hints: A score is twenty.
Four score and seven is four twenties plus seven.
Subtract that number of years from the year of the speech.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7 = 87, and 1863 − 87 = 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

questions.onCorrect: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7 = 87, and 1863 − 87 takes the nation back to the Declaration.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the year of the speech. Subtract the years the phrase names.
That is how many years, not the year the phrase points back to.
That is the Constitution's year. Work out four twenties plus seven and take it from the year of the speech.

questions.prompt: Douglass delivered his attack on slavery at a celebration of American independence, the day after the Fourth of July. Which Greek term names a speaker's use of the right moment and occasion?
hints: It is the term often added to Aristotle's three appeals, and it means the opportune moment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Kairos: the timeliness of a speech, the fit between argument and occasion.

questions.onCorrect: Kairos: the fit between a speech and the moment it is spoken in.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are Aristotle's three proofs. The question asks for the term about timing.

questions.prompt: Lincoln says the war is 'testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.' He reasons from the nation's founding premise to what the war puts at stake. Which appeal is this chiefly?
hints: Look for the appeal named after the Greek for 'word' or 'reason'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Logos: an appeal through reasoning from premise to consequence.

questions.onCorrect: Logos: Lincoln reasons from the nation's founding premise to what the war puts at stake.

questions.prompt: A charity letter opens: 'As a children's nurse for twenty years, I have seen what a missed vaccination can do.' Which appeal does the opening clause make first?

questions.onCorrect: Four. The repeated opening is anaphora, and Dickens keeps it going for ten clauses in the full sentence.

questions.prompt: Lincoln sets 'what we say here' against 'what they did here' in matching grammatical form. Name the figure that balances opposed ideas in parallel structure.
hints: The Greek name means 'setting against'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Antithesis: contrasting ideas placed in parallel form, here saying against doing and 'we' against 'they'.

questions.onCorrect: Antithesis: opposed ideas, saying against doing and “we” against “they”, in matching grammatical form.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.' The terms return in reverse order, A B B A. Name the figure.

questions.prompt: 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people.' Name the figure made of three parallel members.

questions.onCorrect: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three prepositional phrases sharing one noun.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.' Which figure does the repeated opening 'your' create?

questions.prompt: The witches in Macbeth chant 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair.' Which figure is this?
hints: Look at the order of the two repeated words in each half.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus: fair, foul / foul, fair. The reversal suits a play in which appearances invert.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'
