questions.prompt: After Mr Elton's proposal Austen writes: 'Emma sat down to think and be miserable. It was a wretched business indeed!' The second sentence is Emma's own exclamation, in the third person and past tense, with no 'she thought' and no quotation marks. What is this technique called?
hints: Compare it with 'She thought that it was a wretched business'. Which part has been dropped, and what does that make the reported thought?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free indirect discourse, also called free indirect style or speech: the narrator's grammar carries the character's voice.

questions.onCorrect: Free indirect discourse: the narrator's grammar carries the character's voice, with no reporting verb.

misconceptions.feedback: Indirect speech keeps the reporting words: “she thought that”. Here they have been dropped.
Direct speech would use quotation marks and the character's own person.

questions.prompt: (1) “If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.” (2) … Emma sat down to think and be miserable. (3) How she could have been so deceived! Give the number of the sentence that is free indirect discourse.
hints: Direct speech sits inside quotation marks.
Plain narration reports actions from outside.
Look for a character's exclamation in the third person.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sentence 3: Emma's exclamation in the third person and past tense, with no reporting verb. Sentence 1 is direct speech; sentence 2 is narration.

questions.onCorrect: Sentence 3 is Emma's exclamation in the narrator's third person and past tense, with no reporting verb.

misconceptions.feedback: That sentence is in quotation marks, so it is direct speech.
That is plain narration: an action reported from outside.

questions.prompt: Turn the direct thought 'I have been a fool' into free indirect discourse about Emma. Which pronoun replaces 'I'?
hints: Free indirect discourse uses the narrator's grammatical person, not the character's.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'She had been a fool!' The person shifts to the third and the tense moves back, but the exclamation stays Emma's.

questions.onCorrect: “She had been a fool!” The person shifts to the third and the tense moves back, but the exclamation stays Emma's.

misconceptions.feedback: Emma is one person. Choose the third-person pronoun for her.

questions.prompt: Which feature most reliably marks free indirect discourse?
hints: Think about what is missing compared with 'she thought that'.

acceptedIdeas: A character's own exclamations and idiom in third-person past tense, with no reporting verb
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free indirect discourse keeps the narrator's person and tense but drops the reporting verb, so the character's idiom enters the narration directly.

choices.label: A character's own exclamations and idiom in third-person past tense, with no reporting verb
Quotation marks around a character's words
A first-person narrator addressing the reader

questions.onCorrect: Free indirect discourse keeps the narrator's person and tense but drops the reporting verb, so the character's idiom enters the narration.

misconceptions.feedback: Quotation marks mark direct speech, which keeps the character's own person and tense.
A first-person narrator is a different mode. Free indirect discourse stays in the narrator's third person.

questions.prompt: In the eight lines shown from Antony's funeral speech, how many times is Brutus called 'an honourable man'?
hints: Look for the exact phrase with the singular 'man'.
'All honourable men' refers to the conspirators as a group; leave it out.
Count each line that applies the phrase to Brutus, including the one that calls him 'he'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four. Each repetition follows evidence against the charge of ambition, so the praise turns into accusation: verbal irony.

questions.onCorrect: Four. Each repetition follows evidence against the charge of ambition, so the praise turns into accusation.

misconceptions.feedback: Look again for the exact phrase with “man” in the singular: one more line has it.
That counts every line shown. Count only the lines that apply the phrase to Brutus.
“All honourable men” names the conspirators as a group. Leave that line out.

questions.prompt: Romeo, in the tomb, believes Juliet is dead; the audience knows she has taken a sleeping potion and will wake. What kind of irony arises when the audience knows what a character does not?
hints: It is named after the form in which it is most at home: plays.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dramatic irony: the audience's knowledge exceeds the character's, so his words carry a meaning he cannot hear.

questions.onCorrect: Dramatic irony: the audience's knowledge exceeds the character's, so his words carry a meaning he cannot hear.

misconceptions.feedback: Verbal irony lives in a speaker's wording. Here the point is what the audience knows that he does not.
Situational irony is an outcome that reverses an intention. Here the point is unequal knowledge.

questions.prompt: Romeo steps between Mercutio and Tybalt to stop the fight, and Tybalt's thrust under his arm kills Mercutio. The intervention causes the death it was meant to prevent. Which kind of irony is this?
hints: The irony lies in how events turn out, not in what anyone says or knows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Situational irony: the outcome reverses the intention that produced it.

questions.onCorrect: Situational irony: the outcome reverses the intention that produced it.

misconceptions.feedback: Dramatic irony needs an audience that knows more than a character. Here the outcome turns against its cause.
Nobody says the opposite of what they mean. Here an event reverses an intention.

questions.prompt: Poe's narrator insists he is sane while describing a murder in frantic, broken sentences. What term describes a narrator whose account readers have reason to distrust?
hints: It is the opposite of a narrator whose word you can trust.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An unreliable narrator: the telling itself, with its dashes and protests, gives evidence against what it claims.

questions.onCorrect: An unreliable narrator: the telling itself, with its dashes and protests, gives evidence against what it claims.

misconceptions.feedback: Those name kinds of irony. The question asks about a narrator whose account cannot be trusted.
An omniscient narrator knows everything and is trusted. This narrator gives himself away.

questions.prompt: Austen's narrator calls it 'a truth universally acknowledged' that a rich single man 'must be in want of a wife'; the novel shows it is the families who want the man. Which kind of irony does the sentence use: dramatic, situational or verbal?
hints: The irony lives in the wording of a statement.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Verbal irony: the statement says one thing and means its reverse.

questions.onCorrect: Verbal irony: the statement says one thing and means its reverse.

misconceptions.feedback: Dramatic irony needs unequal knowledge between audience and character. Here the wording itself reverses.
No event reverses an intention in this sentence. The wording does.

questions.prompt: In a play, the audience has watched a character poison the wine. The host then raises a glass and toasts his guest's long life. Which kind of irony is at work?
hints: Ask who knows about the poison.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dramatic irony: the audience knows about the poison and the host does not, so his toast means something he cannot hear.

questions.onCorrect: Dramatic irony: the audience knows about the poison and the host does not, so his toast means something he cannot hear.

misconceptions.feedback: No event turns against its cause here. Ask who knows about the poison.
Nobody says the opposite of what they mean. Ask who knows about the poison.

questions.prompt: Romeo and Juliet has five acts. In which act does Freytag place its climax, the high point after which the action turns against the lovers?
hints: Freytag's pyramid puts the climax in the middle of a five-act play.
Find the act in which Romeo kills Tybalt and the lovers part.
Count the acts up to that point.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Act 3. Freytag treats Tybalt's death as the end of the rise and the scene group from 'Gallop apace' to Romeo's farewell as the climax.

questions.onCorrect: Act 3. Freytag ends the rise with Tybalt's death and places the climax from “Gallop apace” to Romeo's farewell.

misconceptions.feedback: Act 1 is the introduction. The climax comes where the rise ends and the fall begins.
Act 5 is the tomb, where the play ends. The climax comes earlier.
Act 2 is still rising. Find the act where Romeo kills Tybalt and the lovers part.
Act 4 already falls. The climax comes just before it.

questions.prompt: Name the part of Freytag's pyramid that introduces the place, the time and the people before the conflict begins.
hints: It comes first and explains the situation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The exposition, Freytag's 'Einleitung' or introduction.

questions.onCorrect: The exposition, Freytag's “Einleitung” or introduction, sets out the world before the action starts.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a later part. The part asked for comes first, before the conflict begins.

questions.prompt: The diagram gives eight scenes of Romeo and Juliet, each opening and closing with a value for the lovers, + or −. A scene turns when its closing value differs from its opening value. How many of the eight scenes turn?
hints: Read each scene's opening and closing sign.
A scene that opens + and closes + does not turn.
Count the scenes whose two signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five: 1.5, 3.1, 3.5, 4.1 and 5.1. The balcony, the wedding and the tomb hold their value.

questions.onCorrect: Five: scenes 1.5, 3.1, 3.5, 4.1 and 5.1 change value. The balcony, the wedding and the tomb hold theirs.

misconceptions.feedback: Check scene 4.1 again: it opens at − and closes at +.
More scenes than that change value. Compare each scene's two signs.
That counts every scene. Count only those whose signs differ.
One of the scenes you counted holds its value. Compare the signs again.

questions.prompt: The diagram plots how high the action has climbed in each of six numbered scenes of a heist story. Which scene is the climax?
hints: Freytag's climax is the highest point of the pyramid.
Compare the heights of the scene markers.
Give the scene's number, counting from the left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Scene 4, the alarm: the action peaks there and every later scene descends.

questions.onCorrect: Scene 4, the alarm: the action peaks there and every later scene descends.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the height, not the scene's number. Give the scene.
Scene 6 is the last scene. The climax is the highest point.
Scene 3 is high, but a later scene is higher.

questions.prompt: In Freytag's scheme, what is the final part of a tragedy, in which the hero falls, called?
hints: The Greek word means an overturning.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The catastrophe, Freytag's 'Katastrophe'; in other plots the same position is called the denouement or resolution.

questions.onCorrect: The catastrophe, Freytag's “Katastrophe”. In other plots the same position is called the denouement or resolution.

misconceptions.feedback: The climax comes earlier, when fortunes turn. The final part comes after it.
The fall comes before the final part. Name the part that closes the play.

questions.prompt: Romeo is banished at the end of 3.1, and Juliet takes the Friar's potion in Act 4. Where do these events sit on Freytag's pyramid?
hints: Do they come before or after the climax?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Falling action: after the climax, events carry the lovers down towards the catastrophe.

questions.onCorrect: Falling action: after the climax, events carry the lovers down towards the catastrophe.

misconceptions.feedback: Rising action comes before the climax. These events come after it.
Exposition opens the play. These events come late in it.

questions.prompt: “The window was broken by Sam.” Say it so that Sam comes first. How many words does your sentence have?
hints: Start with Sam. What did Sam do?
Turn “was broken” into one plain past verb.
Count every word, including “the”.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four: “Sam broke the window.”

questions.onCorrect: Four words: “Sam broke the window.” Putting the actor first drops “was” and “by”.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length of the original. Rewrite it with Sam acting, then count.
Drop both “was” and “by”: “broken” becomes a plain past verb.
You have lost a word. Check that “the” is still there.

questions.prompt: In “The pitch was flooded by the storm”, which word names the actor?
hints: Look inside the “by” phrase.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: storm

questions.onCorrect: The storm did the flooding. In the passive the actor moves into a “by” phrase, and the receiver becomes the subject.

misconceptions.feedback: The pitch receives the action. Find the one that does it.
“Flooded” is the action itself. Ask who or what did it.

questions.prompt: Why does the active version read as stronger?

acceptedIdeas: The reader meets the actor first, and the verb is shorter.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The actor leads and the verb is shorter.

choices.label: The reader meets the actor first, and the verb is shorter.
It is longer, so it carries more detail.

questions.onCorrect: The actor leads and the verb is direct, so the sentence says who did what in fewer words.

misconceptions.feedback: It is shorter, not longer. The extra words in the passive carry nothing.
Not always. The passive suits cases where the actor is unknown or does not matter.

questions.prompt: Which sentence puts the actor in the subject and the action in the verb: “A review of the rules was undertaken by the staff”?
hints: Two things have to change: who leads, and where the action sits.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The staff reviewed the rules.

choices.label: The staff undertook a review of the rules.
The rules were reviewed by the staff.

questions.onCorrect: “Reviewed” turns the buried noun back into a verb, and the staff acts as subject.

misconceptions.feedback: The staff are now the subject, but the action is still buried in a noun.
The verb is restored, but the sentence is still passive, so the receiver leads.

questions.prompt: Which noun buries the verb in “The board gave a refusal of the request”?
hints: Look for an action word that has become a noun.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: refusal

questions.onCorrect: “A refusal” is the action turned into a noun, and “gave” is a weak verb carrying it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Request” names what was refused. Find the noun that is really an action.
“Board” is the actor. The buried verb is hidden in an action noun.

questions.prompt: You are choosing a mountain guide. Which sentence makes you trust her most before she says anything else?
hints: Which sentence tells you something about the speaker herself?

acceptedIdeas: “I have led this route forty times.”
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her forty trips of the route earn trust.

choices.label: “I have led this route forty times.”

questions.onCorrect: Her record is what earns trust. A speaker's own experience can persuade before any argument begins.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a guess about the weather. It tells you nothing about her.
That is a fact anyone could state. It says nothing about her experience.

questions.prompt: “Because the budget has doubled while results have not, the programme should be reviewed.” Which Greek-named proof is at work: ethos, pathos or logos?
hints: Does the sentence reason, or does it move the audience?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: logos

questions.onCorrect: The sentence reasons from a fact to a conclusion. That is argument carried by the words themselves.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing here is about who the speaker is or why she should be trusted.
No feeling is aroused. The sentence moves from a fact to a conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why does “As a lifelong farmer” count as ethos?

acceptedIdeas: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It tells the audience who is speaking and why to trust her.

choices.label: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.
It gives a reason for the policy.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos works through the speaker's character and standing. Experience is part of what makes her believable.

misconceptions.feedback: It arouses no fear. It tells you who is speaking.
A reason would be an argument. This phrase only says who the speaker is.

questions.prompt: “Think of the families who lost everything in the flood.” Which appeal does the sentence rely on?
hints: What does the sentence ask the audience to imagine?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos

questions.onCorrect: It asks the audience to picture a loss. That works on feeling, not on reasoning or on the speaker's standing.

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence says nothing about the speaker. Ask what it asks the audience to do.
No premise leads to a conclusion here. The sentence offers an image.

questions.prompt: Which best describes kairos?
hints: The word means the right moment.

acceptedIdeas: Fitting an argument to its moment and place.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fitting an argument to its moment and place.

choices.label: Fitting an argument to its moment and place.
Repeating a word at the start of clauses.
Arguing from a premise to a consequence.

questions.onCorrect: Kairos is the opportune moment: a speech fits its occasion and may use the place itself as evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a figure of repetition, not a proof. Kairos is about timing.
That describes reasoning, not timing.

questions.prompt: Your friend says “Get a dog: mine makes me so happy.” How many of these does she say aloud? (1) You should get a dog. (2) Her dog makes her happy. (3) What makes her happy will make you happy.
hints: Read her exact words, one statement at a time.
Which statements can you find in what she said?
One statement is a belief that her advice relies on.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: statements 1 and 2. Statement 3 is the belief her advice depends on, and she never says it.

questions.onCorrect: Two: the advice and the fact. The link between them is unstated, yet her advice only follows if it holds.

misconceptions.feedback: Read her words again. One of these is a belief she assumes without saying.
She says more than the advice. Check what reason she gives.
She says at least her advice. Check each statement against her words.

questions.prompt: “The pavement is wet, so it has rained.” Which words give the grounds?
hints: Which part can you check by looking?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: the pavement is wet

questions.onCorrect: The grounds are the observed fact. “It has rained” is the claim, and the link between them is the warrant.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the conclusion drawn from the fact, so it is the claim. Find the fact itself.
That would be a general rule linking fact to conclusion. Grounds are the particular fact.

questions.prompt: Why is “forecasts are usually right” a warrant and not grounds?

acceptedIdeas: It is a general rule that links the fact to the claim.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a general rule linking the particular fact to the claim.

choices.label: It is a general rule that links the fact to the claim.
It comes last in the sentence.

questions.onCorrect: A warrant is a general rule. Grounds are the particular fact it lets you rely on.

misconceptions.feedback: Position does not decide the role. Ask whether the statement is a fact or a rule.
A qualifier can sit in any statement. The question is what job the statement does.

questions.prompt: In “The tournament will almost certainly go ahead, unless the pitch floods”, which part is the rebuttal?
hints: Which part says when the claim would not hold?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: unless the pitch floods

questions.onCorrect: The rebuttal names the condition under which the claim would fail.

misconceptions.feedback: That words how sure the writer is. Look for the part that says what would make the claim fail.
That is the claim itself. A rebuttal limits it from outside.

questions.prompt: In “Buses are usually on time, unless snow falls”, which word opens the rebuttal?
hints: Which word introduces what could stop the claim holding?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: unless

questions.onCorrect: The rebuttal names the condition under which the claim would fail, and here it opens with “unless”.

misconceptions.feedback: “Usually” measures how often the claim holds. A rebuttal names what could defeat it.
That is part of the claim. A rebuttal limits it from outside.

questions.prompt: “The dog chases the ball.” Retell it as yesterday's story. How many of its five words change?
hints: Say the sentence with “yesterday” at the start.
Change each word in turn and see which one you have to alter.
Nouns and “the” do not change with time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One: only “chases” becomes “chased”.

questions.onCorrect: Only “chases” changes, to “chased”. The word that shifts with time is the one that holds the clause together.

misconceptions.feedback: Say it with “yesterday” in front. One of the words has to change.
Nouns and articles keep their form. Only the word for what happens shifts.
Most words stay put when the time changes. Test them one at a time.

questions.prompt: Which word is the finite verb in “The old man walked home slowly”?
hints: Put the sentence into the present. Which word changes?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: walked

questions.onCorrect: “Walked” carries the tense. It would be “walks” in the present, and “the old man” is who does it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Old” describes the man and does not change with time. Find the word that would change in the present.
“Slowly” says how it happens. It stays the same in any tense.
“Home” names where he went. It stays the same in any tense.

questions.prompt: Why is “fierce” a complement and not an object?

acceptedIdeas: It says what the subject is like, and nothing receives an action.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Was” links the subject to a description, so “fierce” is a complement.

choices.label: It says what the subject is like, and nothing receives an action.
It is the last word in the clause.
It is a single word, and objects need two.

questions.onCorrect: A complement says what the subject is or is like. An object receives the verb's action.

misconceptions.feedback: Position is not the test. Ask whether the word receives an action or describes the subject.
Objects can be one word too, as in “shook the roof”. Ask what the word does.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a dependent clause?
hints: Which one would leave you waiting for the rest of the sentence?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: when the rain stopped

choices.label: The rain stopped and the sun came out

questions.onCorrect: “When” makes the clause lean on another one. It has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That could be a sentence on its own, so it is independent.
Both clauses here could stand alone. Look for a clause that opens with a word that makes it wait for more.

questions.prompt: “I came, I saw, I conquered.” How many of its parts begin with “I”?
hints: Split the line at each comma.
Look at the first word of each part.
Count the parts that open with the same word.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: each of the three short parts begins with “I”.

questions.onCorrect: Three. Starting every part the same way makes the sentence move like a march.

misconceptions.feedback: Check each part of the line, not only the first.
There is one more part after the second comma.
Count the parts that begin with the word, not the word itself wherever it appears.

questions.prompt: In “Every day, every hour, every minute”, which word repeats at the start of each part?
hints: Compare the first word of each part.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: every

questions.onCorrect: “Every” opens each part. Repeating the opening word is anaphora, and it draws the eye to what changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the parts that change. Find the word that stays the same each time.

questions.prompt: “Never let a fool kiss you or a kiss fool you.” In the second half, which of the two repeated words comes first?
hints: Compare the two halves. Which word leads in each?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: kiss

questions.onCorrect: “Kiss” comes first in the second half, “fool” in the first. The terms return in reverse order: chiasmus.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the order of the first half. In the second half the order flips.

questions.prompt: Which line is built as an antithesis?
hints: Look for opposed ideas placed in parallel form.

acceptedIdeas: “To err is human; to forgive, divine.”
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “To err is human; to forgive, divine.”

choices.label: “To err is human; to forgive, divine.”
“Fair is foul, and foul is fair.”

questions.onCorrect: Opposed ideas, human and divine, sit in matching grammatical form.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a series of three parallel short parts. It is not built on opposition.
That reverses the order of its terms rather than setting opposed ideas in a matching frame.

questions.prompt: Your friend watches the rain soak her picnic and says “Wonderful weather.” What does she mean?
hints: What has just happened to her picnic?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She means the opposite of what she says.

questions.onCorrect: She says one thing and means the opposite, and you can hear the gap between the two.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at the picnic. Her words and the scene do not agree.
Nothing in her words or the scene suggests change. Ask what the rain has done to her picnic.

questions.prompt: A friend says “Nice parking” about a car wedged across two bays. Which word means the opposite of what she thinks?
hints: Which word praises something she does not praise?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: nice

questions.onCorrect: “Nice” says the opposite of her view. The gap is plain because everyone can see the car.

misconceptions.feedback: “Parking” is accurate. Find the word whose meaning she reverses.

questions.prompt: How many of these are dramatic irony? (1) The audience knows the letter is forged, but the heroine does not. (2) A bakery runs out of bread on its opening day. (3) The audience sees the villain pocket the key as the hero says “I trust you.”
hints: Ask of each statement who knows what.
Dramatic irony needs the audience to know more than a character.
One statement is about an unexpected outcome, not about knowledge.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: statements 1 and 3, where the audience knows what a character does not. Statement 2 is an outcome that reverses an expectation.

questions.onCorrect: Two. Dramatic irony depends on unequal knowledge, so the audience hears meaning the character cannot.

misconceptions.feedback: Check each statement for something the audience knows that a character does not.
One of these is an outcome reversing an expectation, which is another kind of irony.
Look for statements where the audience knows more than a character.

questions.prompt: A fire station burns to the ground. What kind of irony is that: verbal, dramatic or situational?
hints: Does anyone say or know anything here, or does an event simply turn out oddly?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: situational

questions.onCorrect: Situational irony: the outcome turns against the purpose of the thing it happens to.

misconceptions.feedback: Dramatic irony needs the audience to know more than a character. Here an outcome turns against what you would expect.
Nobody says the opposite of what they mean. Here an event reverses an expectation.

questions.prompt: Split “We waited, the bus never came” into the fewest complete sentences. How many sentences do you get?
hints: Read each half of the comma aloud on its own.
Does each half make sense standing alone?
Count the halves that could be sentences.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: “We waited.” and “The bus never came.”

questions.onCorrect: Two. Each half is a full clause that could stand alone, and a comma is too weak to join them.

misconceptions.feedback: A comma does not make one sentence out of two. Try reading each half on its own.
Each half is already a complete sentence. You do not need to split further.

questions.prompt: Which mark links two clauses as one thought, without a conjunction?
hints: Think of the mark that sits between a comma and a full stop in strength.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: semicolon

questions.onCorrect: A semicolon links two full clauses as one thought and leaves their relation unstated.

misconceptions.feedback: A comma on its own is too weak to hold two full clauses.
A full stop keeps the clauses apart. The question asks for a mark that links them.

questions.prompt: Why does the semicolon need no conjunction here?

acceptedIdeas: It already links two full clauses as one thought.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A semicolon links two complete clauses without a conjunction.

choices.label: It already links two full clauses as one thought.
It is just a heavier comma.

questions.onCorrect: A semicolon is a full link between clauses: it joins them without saying how they relate.

misconceptions.feedback: A comma cannot do this job, so the semicolon is not just a stronger version of it.
Semicolons do separate list items that contain commas, but they also join clauses.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
hints: Check that each side of the semicolon could stand as a sentence.

acceptedIdeas: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.

choices.label: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.
The match was cancelled; because the pitch was flooded.

questions.onCorrect: Both halves are full clauses, so a semicolon can join them without a conjunction.

misconceptions.feedback: “Because the pitch was flooded” cannot stand alone, so a semicolon cannot join it.
The words before the semicolon are not a full clause. A semicolon needs complete clauses on both sides.

questions.prompt: Clap along to “Twinkle, twinkle, little star”, once on each beat. How many claps do you make?
hints: Say the line aloud and tap along.
Tap harder on the strong syllables.
Count only the strong taps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four: TWIN-kle TWIN-kle LIT-tle STAR, one on each stressed syllable.

questions.onCorrect: Four. You clapped on the strong syllables only, and that regular pulse is what metre counts.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every syllable. You clap only on the strong ones.
There is a clap on each of the four strong syllables. Say it again and tap.
That counts words and syllables together. Clap only where the stress falls.

questions.prompt: “com-PARE” is an iamb. Does its beat fall on the first or the second syllable?
hints: Say “compare” and listen for the louder syllable.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: second

questions.onCorrect: The beat falls on the second syllable. An iamb is a weak syllable followed by a strong one.

misconceptions.feedback: Say the word aloud. The strong syllable is the later one.

questions.prompt: Why does “They also serve who only stand and waite” count as iambic pentameter?

acceptedIdeas: It has ten syllables in five weak-strong pairs.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has ten syllables in five weak-strong pairs.

choices.label: It has ten syllables in five weak-strong pairs.

questions.onCorrect: Five iambs make ten syllables, with the beats on every second one.

misconceptions.feedback: The line has eight words, and words are not what the metre counts. Count syllables and pairs.
Several words have two syllables. Metre counts the pattern of weak and strong.

questions.prompt: Which line has an extra unstressed syllable after its last beat?
hints: Count the syllables in each line. Which has one too many?

acceptedIdeas: To be, or not to be, that is the question
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To be, or not to be, that is the question

choices.label: To be, or not to be, that is the question
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
They also serve who only stand and waite

questions.onCorrect: It has eleven syllables, and “-tion” trails after the last beat.

misconceptions.feedback: That line has ten syllables and ends on a beat.
That line has ten syllables and ends on a beat.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in a line of iambic tetrameter?
hints: How many feet does tetrameter have?
How many syllables does an iamb have?
Multiply the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four iambs of two syllables each make eight.

questions.onCorrect: Eight: four feet of two syllables each. The count of feet names the metre.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of feet. Each foot has two syllables.
That is pentameter, with five feet. This line has four.
That is trimeter, with three feet.

questions.prompt: A friend retells her day: “I walked in and everyone went quiet.” Where is she in relation to the story?
hints: Who does the word “I” point to?

acceptedIdeas: She is a character in it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She says “I”, so she is a character in it.

choices.label: She is a character in it.

questions.onCorrect: She says “I”, so she is inside the story she tells. Where the narrator stands changes what we learn.

misconceptions.feedback: She says “I” and describes her own entrance, so she is part of the events.
She is the one telling it. Ask who the “I” is.

questions.prompt: A narrator says “we trudged home”. Is that first, second or third person?
hints: Is the narrator one of the people described?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: first

questions.onCorrect: “We” includes the narrator, so the narration is in the first person.

misconceptions.feedback: Third person calls the characters “he”, “she” or “they”. This narrator is among the “we”.
Second person addresses the reader as “you”. Who is the “we”?

questions.prompt: In free indirect discourse, whose grammatical person and tense does the sentence use: the narrator's or the character's?
hints: Compare it with direct speech, which uses the character's own person.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: narrator

questions.onCorrect: The sentence keeps the narrator's person and tense, while the character's words and feeling show through.

misconceptions.feedback: The character's own grammar would be direct speech. Whose voice is telling the story here?

questions.prompt: Why is “What a dreadful day it had been!” free indirect discourse and not plain narration?

acceptedIdeas: It keeps Anna's own exclamation inside the narrator's grammar.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps Anna's own exclamation inside the narrator's grammar.

choices.label: It keeps Anna's own exclamation inside the narrator's grammar.
It is in the first person.

questions.onCorrect: Third person and past tense come from the narrator, while the exclamation is Anna's own.

misconceptions.feedback: Quotation marks would make it direct speech. This sentence has none.
It says “it had been”, so the narrator's third person and past tense remain.

questions.prompt: Turn Tom's direct thought “I am so tired!” into free indirect discourse. Which two words replace “I am”?
hints: The narrator speaks about Tom, not as Tom.
Both the person and the tense shift.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: he was

questions.onCorrect: “He was so tired!” moves the person to the third and the tense back, but the exclamation stays Tom's.

misconceptions.feedback: The person has moved, but the tense has not. The narrator's tense is the past.
“I” is Tom's own person. The narrator speaks of him in the third person.

questions.prompt: “Roses are red / Violets are blue / Sugar is sweet / And so are you.” Which line number rhymes with line 2?
hints: Say the last word of each line.
Which ending sounds like “blue”?
Give that line's number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Line 4: “blue” and “you” rhyme.

questions.onCorrect: Line 4: blue and you end on the same sound. Rhyme is how a verse tells you where its lines belong together.

misconceptions.feedback: Line 1 ends “red”. Listen for the line that ends like “blue”.
Line 3 ends “sweet”. Find the ending that sounds like “blue”.
Line 2 is the line you are matching. Find another one.

questions.prompt: A quatrain rhymes ABAB. Which line number rhymes with line 1?
hints: Each letter stands for one rhyme sound.
Which lines carry the letter A?
Give the line that is not line 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Line 3: the letter A appears on lines 1 and 3.

questions.onCorrect: Line 3. Each letter is one rhyme sound, and lines that share a letter rhyme.

misconceptions.feedback: Line 2 is B. Look for the other line marked A.
Line 4 is B. Look for the other line marked A.
Line 1 is the line you are matching. Find the other one.

questions.prompt: In a Petrarchan sonnet, after which line does the volta usually fall?
hints: How long is the octave?
The turn comes where the octave gives way to the sestet.
Count the lines of the octave.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After line 8, where the octave gives way to the sestet.

questions.onCorrect: After line 8: the octave sets out the problem and the sestet answers it.

misconceptions.feedback: The sestet has six lines. The turn comes where the octave ends.
That is the last line of the poem. Find where the first part ends.
That ends the first quatrain. In this form the first part is longer.

questions.prompt: A Petrarchan sestet rhymes CDECDE. How many different rhyme sounds does it use?
hints: Each letter is one rhyme sound.
Ignore repeats of a letter.
Count the distinct letters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: C, D and E.

questions.onCorrect: Three: the letters C, D and E repeat, so the sestet has only three rhyme sounds.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts lines. Count the distinct letters.
Check the scheme again: there is one more letter than that.
Count each letter once, even when it recurs.

questions.prompt: Say “Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.” How many words begin with the p sound?
hints: Say it aloud and listen to how each word begins.
Ignore the small words in between.
Count the words that start with the p sound.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six: Peter, Piper, picked, peck, pickled and peppers.

questions.onCorrect: Six. The same sound opening nearby words is what the ear picks up as a pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: Check each word again. One more begins with the same sound.
Count only words that begin with the sound. “Of” and “a” do not.
Listen to every word that opens with the sound, not just the first few.

questions.prompt: How many of these pairs alliterate: knee and nose; cat and city; phone and fish?
hints: Say each pair aloud.
Listen for the first sound, not the first letter.
“Phone” and “fish” begin the same way, but check the others.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: knee and nose share the n sound, and phone and fish share the f sound. Cat and city start with k and s.

questions.onCorrect: Two. Alliteration follows sound, not spelling: knee and nose match, and so do phone and fish.

misconceptions.feedback: Say each pair aloud. Spelling can mislead you in both directions.
Say “cat” and “city” aloud. Do they begin with the same sound?
Listen to the first sound of each word, not its first letter.

questions.prompt: Which word marks the comparison in “Her voice was like honey”?
hints: Which small word says that two things are being compared?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: like

questions.onCorrect: “Like” announces the comparison. That makes it a simile, and without it the line would be a metaphor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the thing she is compared with. Find the small word that announces the comparison.
That is what is being described. Find the word that announces the comparison.

questions.prompt: In Wordsworth's “I wandered lonely as a Cloud”, which is the vehicle?
hints: Which word names the thing borrowed to make a picture?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: a Cloud

questions.onCorrect: The vehicle is the borrowed image. The cloud carries a picture of drifting alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The speaker is what is being described. The vehicle is the image borrowed to describe him.
“Lonely” is the quality the two share. The vehicle is the thing borrowed for the picture.

questions.prompt: A film's tension in five scenes runs 1, 3, 6, 9, 5. Which scene is the tensest?
hints: Read the five numbers in order.
Which number is the largest?
Give that number's place in the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Scene 4: its tension of 9 is the highest.

questions.onCorrect: Scene 4. The peak is the point where the story stops building and starts to ease.

misconceptions.feedback: Scene 5 comes after the peak. Find the scene with the highest number.
That is the tension, not the scene number. Give the scene.
Scene 3 is high, but another scene is higher.

questions.prompt: At which part of Freytag's pyramid do the protagonist's fortunes stop rising and start to fall?
hints: Think of the peak of the pyramid.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: climax

questions.onCorrect: The climax is the highest point of the pyramid. Before it fortunes rise, and after it they fall.

misconceptions.feedback: The rise leads up to that point. Name the point itself.
Those come after the high point. Name the point where the turn happens.

questions.prompt: A story's three scenes run: + to −, − to +, + to +. How many of them turn?
hints: Write each scene's opening sign and closing sign.
A scene turns when the two signs differ.
Count the scenes whose signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the first and the second change value. The third opens and closes at +.

questions.onCorrect: Two. A scene turns only when its closing value differs from its opening value.

misconceptions.feedback: The third scene opens and closes at the same value, so it holds.
Check each scene's two signs: more than one differs.
Compare each scene's opening and closing signs.

questions.prompt: Another story's four scenes run: − to +, + to +, + to −, − to −. How many of them turn?
hints: Write each scene's opening sign and closing sign.
A scene turns when the two signs differ.
Count the scenes whose signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the first and third change value.

questions.onCorrect: Two: the first and third change value, while the second and fourth hold theirs.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare each scene's two signs. Some are the same at both ends.
The last scene opens and closes at the same value, so it does not turn.
More than one scene changes value. Compare each scene's signs.

questions.prompt: Why is scene 3 the climax rather than scene 6?

acceptedIdeas: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall after it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall afterwards.

choices.label: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall after it.

questions.onCorrect: The climax is the highest point: the story builds up to it and falls away afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: Position is not the test. Ask where the heights stop rising.
Nothing here measures how long a scene lasts. Look at the heights.

flashcards.front: In 'Thou art more lovely and more temperate', what grammatical function does 'more lovely and more temperate' serve after the linking verb 'art'?
flashcards.back: A subject complement: after a linking verb it describes the subject, 'thou'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A subject complement: after a linking verb it describes the subject, 'thou'.

flashcards.front: How many finite verbs are in 'When I consider how my light is spent, I fondly ask'? Count 'is spent' as one verb.
flashcards.back: Three: 'consider', 'is spent' and 'ask'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'consider', 'is spent' and 'ask'.

flashcards.front: Which mark joins two independent clauses in one sentence without a conjunction and leaves their relation unstated?
flashcards.back: A semicolon. A colon would claim that the second clause explains the first.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A semicolon. A colon would claim that the second clause explains the first.

flashcards.front: What must the words before a colon form?
flashcards.back: A complete (independent) clause. 'The reasons were: cost and delay' fails this test.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A complete (independent) clause. 'The reasons were: cost and delay' fails this test.

flashcards.front: Unbury the verb in 'We had a discussion about the budget' to get 'We discussed the budget'. How many words are saved?
flashcards.back: Seven words become four; three are saved.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Seven words become four; three are saved.

flashcards.front: In 'The window was broken', which participant in the action has the passive left out?
flashcards.back: The agent, or actor: the sentence never says who broke the window.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The agent, or actor: the sentence never says who broke the window.

flashcards.front: In Toulmin's model, which element limits the force of a claim with words such as 'probably' or 'in most cases'?
flashcards.back: The qualifier: it states how strongly the claim is made.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The qualifier: it states how strongly the claim is made.

flashcards.front: Which Toulmin element states the conditions under which a claim would not hold?
flashcards.back: The rebuttal, sometimes called the reservation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rebuttal, sometimes called the reservation.

flashcards.front: How many years is 'four score and seven'?
flashcards.back: Four twenties make eighty; add seven.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four twenties make eighty; add seven.

flashcards.front: Which of Aristotle's three appeals works through the emotions of the audience?
flashcards.back: Pathos: persuasion through the feelings a speech arouses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos: persuasion through the feelings a speech arouses.

flashcards.front: 'We do not live to eat; we eat to live.' Name the figure that reverses the order of the repeated words.
flashcards.back: Chiasmus, or more strictly antimetabole: live, eat / eat, live.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus, or more strictly antimetabole: live, eat / eat, live.

flashcards.front: What is a series of three parallel members, as in 'I came, I saw, I conquered', called?
flashcards.back: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three short clauses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three short clauses.

flashcards.front: How many syllables are in Milton's 'They also serve who only stand and waite'?
flashcards.back: Ten: they / al / so / serve / who / on / ly / stand / and / waite. A regular iambic pentameter line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ten: they / al / so / serve / who / on / ly / stand / and / waite. A regular iambic pentameter line.

flashcards.front: Name the metrical foot with the pattern unstressed then stressed.
flashcards.back: The iamb, as in 'com-PARE'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The iamb, as in 'com-PARE'.

flashcards.front: How many words in Keats's 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness' begin with the m sound?
flashcards.back: Two: 'mists' and 'mellow'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'mists' and 'mellow'.

flashcards.front: In I. A. Richards's terms, what is the subject a metaphor describes called, as opposed to its vehicle?
flashcards.back: The tenor. In 'Juliet is the sun', Juliet is the tenor and the sun the vehicle.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tenor. In 'Juliet is the sun', Juliet is the tenor and the sun the vehicle.

flashcards.front: How many lines are in the sestet of a Petrarchan sonnet?
flashcards.back: Six; the octave has eight.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six; the octave has eight.

flashcards.front: What is the Italian term for the turn in a sonnet's argument?
flashcards.back: The volta: the point where the argument changes direction.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The volta: the point where the argument changes direction.

flashcards.front: In which grammatical person does a narrator write who is also a character and says 'I'?
flashcards.back: First person: the narrator is inside the story and says 'I'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: First person: the narrator is inside the story and says 'I'.

flashcards.front: What does free indirect discourse leave out that indirect speech such as 'she thought that it was hopeless' includes?
flashcards.back: The reporting verb (the reporting clause 'she thought that').

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reporting verb (the reporting clause 'she thought that').

flashcards.front: Which kind of irony occurs when a speaker says the opposite of what is meant?
flashcards.back: Verbal irony: the words say one thing and mean another.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Verbal irony: the words say one thing and mean another.

flashcards.front: Which kind of irony arises when an outcome reverses the intention that produced it?
flashcards.back: Situational irony: events turn against the purpose that set them going.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Situational irony: events turn against the purpose that set them going.

flashcards.front: A story's five scenes run: + to +, + to −, − to −, − to +, + to +. How many scenes turn?
flashcards.back: Two: the second (+ to −) and the fourth (− to +).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the second (+ to −) and the fourth (− to +).

flashcards.front: Name the part of Freytag's pyramid between the climax and the catastrophe.
flashcards.back: The falling action, which Freytag calls the return or fall.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The falling action, which Freytag calls the return or fall.

lines.text: My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun;
Coral is far more red, than her lips red:
If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun;
If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.
I have seen roses damask’d, red and white,
But no such roses see I in her cheeks;
And in some perfumes is there more delight
Than in the breath that from my mistress reeks.
I love to hear her speak, yet well I know
That music hath a far more pleasing sound:
I grant I never saw a goddess go;
My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground:
And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare,
As any she belied with false compare.

lines.text: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature’s changing course untrimm’d:
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st,
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
